id_and_class.theory_title: Hill's Representationalism: Qualia’s Appearance and Reality
id_and_class.summary: Christopher S. Hill holds that all awareness is representational: to be aware of something is to be in a state that represents it, and phenomenal experience is a rich, mostly nonconceptual form of such representation. Because representations can misrepresent, he applies the appearance/reality distinction to qualia themselves, so introspection need not reveal what qualia really are, which removes the evidential base of arguments for property dualism.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Qualia as Represented Appearances, Not Self-Revealing Essences

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Phenomenal consciousness is experiential representation: a fine-grained, typically nonconceptual presentation of colors, sounds, bodily conditions, and emotions. Qualia are ways things look, feel, or otherwise appear.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Hill defends materialism by denying that introspection reveals the intrinsic nature of qualia, not by identifying qualia with brain states as his earlier type materialism did. McLaughlin argues the two positions are compatible.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not specified (Hill gives no emergence account; consciousness is a kind of representation within a physicalist ontology)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Whenever a subject is aware of something, it is in a mental state that represents it, so intentionality is the basis of awareness. Introspective awareness of one’s own states takes the form of belief rather than direct acquaintance.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Qualia are appearances that can differ from how things are in themselves. Visual qualia are relational properties of external objects, and pain represents a disturbance in the body, so qualia sit in the body and the world rather than in the head.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Physical brains and bodies, representational states (including nonconceptual ones), and external objects and bodily conditions with relational appearance properties.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Introspection gives vivid access to how things appear but is not metaphysically transparent and can be mistaken. Hill draws heavily on vision science and neuroscience rather than intuition alone.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Hill distinguishes six forms of consciousness: agent, propositional, introspective, relational, phenomenal, and experiential. He argues several classic arguments trade on confusing phenomenal consciousness with introspective awareness of it.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal; introspective; perceptual (vision, pain, emotion); six distinguished forms of consciousness
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: The appearance/reality distinction applied to qualia: because awareness of qualia is representational, the way qualia appear in introspection need not be the way they are.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Qualia are located in the body and the world, as represented bodily conditions and relational properties of external objects, rather than as inner mental objects.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Hill has written on sensory integration and the unity of consciousness, but the representational theory itself does not hinge on a binding mechanism.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Experience represents features more finely than the subject’s concepts can capture; even a demonstrative like ‘that shade’ presupposes a prior experiential presentation.
core_claims_and_evidence: If an agent is aware of X, the agent is in a mental state that represents X.
Experience is more fine-grained than available concepts, so phenomenal awareness is typically nonconceptual.
Since representations can misrepresent, the way qualia appear need not reveal their intrinsic nature.
The knowledge, conceivability, and modal arguments against physicalism all assume introspection reveals phenomenal properties as they are, an assumption Hill rejects.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical argument informed by cognitive science and vision science

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: Hill applies results from vision science to visual awareness and draws on neuroscience for pain and emotion.
empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Locating visual qualia in relational properties of external objects runs into trouble with hallucination and illusion, where those objects are absent (Bernier). Byrne questions whether the perceptual account of pain covers cases where pain seems to outrun any represented bodily disturbance. Denying that introspection is accurate about qualia deflates the very datum most theories of consciousness try to explain.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Critics ask whether representational structure explains phenomenal character or only accompanies and organizes it. Reviewers of Perceptual Experience note it treats non-visual senses one at a time and does not engage multisensory interaction.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Consistent with physicalism and offered as a rival to the phenomenal-concept strategy: where type-B materialists grant that introspection is accurate and explain the gap through special concepts, Hill denies the accuracy assumption.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Hill’s early type materialism held that silicon androids cannot have sensations, but he has since moved to representationalism and its verdict on machines is not settled.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since Hill’s view is physicalist, conscious representation depends on a functioning physical system and does not outlast it.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: The view is naturalistic and gives consciousness no cosmic role.
